clinicalPearls: Breakdown of skeletal muscle releases intracellular contents, notably myoglobin, potassium, phosphate and creatine kinase, into the circulation
The classic triad is muscle pain, weakness and dark (tea-coloured) urine, though many patients lack all three
A markedly raised creatine kinase is the key laboratory finding
Acute kidney injury from myoglobin, and life-threatening hyperkalaemia, are the main dangers
Causes are diverse, including crush and trauma, prolonged immobility, extreme exertion, seizures, drugs, toxins, ischaemia and metabolic myopathies
Early and generous intravenous fluid resuscitation to maintain urine output is the cornerstone of treatment
reference.pathophysiology: Rhabdomyolysis occurs when injury to skeletal muscle disrupts the sarcolemma and releases myoglobin and other intracellular constituents. Myoglobin is filtered by the kidney where it causes tubular obstruction, direct tubular toxicity and renal vasoconstriction, producing acute kidney injury, particularly when the patient is volume-depleted and the urine is acidic. Release of potassium and phosphate and sequestration of calcium in damaged muscle cause dangerous electrolyte disturbances, while a compartment syndrome can both cause and result from the muscle injury.
additionalDifferentials: Acute kidney injury of another cause
additionalInvestigations: Serum creatine kinase and serial trends
Renal function, potassium, phosphate and calcium
Urinalysis showing blood on dipstick without red cells (myoglobinuria)
Investigation of the underlying cause, including compartment pressures if indicated
redFlags: Oliguria or established acute kidney injury
Very high or rising creatine kinase with volume depletion
reference.prognosis: With prompt fluid resuscitation many patients avoid or recover from kidney injury; prognosis worsens with severe hyperkalaemia, established renal failure or the underlying precipitating condition.
pitfalls: Missing hyperkalaemia as an immediate threat
Attributing dark urine to haematuria without checking for myoglobinuria
management: Give early, generous intravenous fluid resuscitation to maintain a high urine output and prevent myoglobin-induced acute kidney injury
Identify, remove and treat the precipitating cause such as crush injury, drugs, toxins, prolonged immobility or seizures
Detect and treat life-threatening hyperkalaemia urgently, with continuous ECG monitoring for hyperkalaemic changes
Correct associated electrolyte disturbances, treating symptomatic hypocalcaemia but otherwise avoiding calcium
Monitor serial creatine kinase, renal function and urine output, and institute renal replacement therapy for refractory hyperkalaemia, acidosis or fluid overload
Assess for and decompress compartment syndrome with fasciotomy where present
